top_choice_rationale: P002 (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) rests on three separable, datable building blocks: time-dependent pricing, staggered contracts with an interest-rate rule, and the microfounded welfare-based policy framework. Each has 25 to 40 years of extension, criticism and use, and the framework is the common language of monetary policy analysis. I would confine the citation to nominal-rigidity theory, policy rules and the welfare-based framework, with no claim about forecasting or the Phillips-curve slope. That answers the post-2008 and 2021-23 inflation concerns on the wording side. The main weakness is attribution: eight names are credited, and a three-person cut omits Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets. I judge this a choice about which layer to honour, not a flaw in the originating contributions. P003 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) is second because it has the coherent credit unit and the most checkable identification, provided the citation is limited to the trade-shock and local-labour-market evidence. P001 follows for its clean two-person credit line, with reservations about the uncredited Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum lineage and functional-form dependence of the welfare gains. P004 follows, given the partly observational identification, the partial overlap with the 2024 prize and the contestable third name. No award is last because several proposals are mature, separable and defensible on the common criteria.
recusal_note: I am a frequent co-author of Per Krusell (secretary) and a co-author of John Hassler (chair), and an IIES colleague of both. Krusell supports P002 and Hassler lists B014 as an alternative. None of Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Helpman, Melitz, Persson, Tabellini or Besley appears as a documented co-author. My long-running collaborators (Aghion, Bergeaud, Klenow, Li) are not credited on any ranked proposal. My macroeconomics and growth field is close to P002, which may bias my sense of how crowded the area is. Disclosed, not adjudicated.
